Moving into a smaller flat was supposed to be a straightforward step: fewer rooms to clean, lower bills, and hopefully, a fresh start. But as I sat on the bare floor, surrounded by towering boxes that seemed to fill every available corner, the reality hit me. These boxes, each carefully labelled ‘keep’, blocked any real sense of space or order. (37) Many weren’t even full; just a collection of odds and ends accumulated over years, boxes filled out of habit rather than intention. I realised that keeping everything wasn’t just impractical — it was impossible.

Among the jumble was a box that puzzled me more than most. Inside, I found a small old umbrella, a gift from years ago, never opened, never used. It had been saved ‘just in case’ it might come in handy one day, but as I held it, I couldn’t recall when or why I thought that day would come. (38) This object became a symbol of the many possessions stored not for their use but for an undefined future, making it harder to make decisions when space was so limited.

While sorting through these items, I heard about a local swap and repair event happening nearby. It wasn’t just about throwing things away — it promised to give unwanted belongings a second chance, either to be reused by someone else or fixed if broken. (39) This idea felt more hopeful, a practical alternative to simply discarding decades of material habits.

At the event, I nervously carried a bag of assorted objects — a chipped mug, a worn-out scarf, and an old lamp I assumed no one else would want. To my surprise, the lamp was quickly snapped up by another visitor who said it was just what she needed for her study. (40) That was different from my expectation — it made me reconsider what I thought was useless or sentimental, highlighting that others could value items in ways I hadn’t imagined.

I also brought along a small, hand-knitted blanket that reminded me of my grandmother. It had little practical use and took up valuable space, yet it seemed impossible to let go. (41) I decided it was a rare exception, a piece kept not for function but for emotional connection, a deliberate choice rather than a mere consequence of habit.

Returning home from the event, I started to form a clearer rule for judging what deserved space in the smaller flat. It wasn’t about emptying shelves or adopting minimalism blindly, but about recognising when something had a definite purpose or personal meaning. (42) This approach wasn’t quick or easy, but it gave me a way to live more deliberately within the limitations of my new home.

Later that evening, I placed a small box on a newly cleared shelf, filled only with items that earned their place by this standard. It wasn’t perfect — there were still pieces whose exact value was uncertain, but that was alright. (37) Instead of aiming for a completely clutter-free life, I found a balance between practical needs and the imperfections that make a home feel lived in.
